extracted.intended_audience: novelists, critics, and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying narrative methods (dramatic vs pictorial/omniscient) in novel-writing: when to use a narrator, when to present scenes dramatically, and how to balance setting, point of view, and method with the subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of narrator only when subject requires
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the presence of a seer and a recorder is made a value in itself, contributing definitely to the effect of the subject, he is better dispensed with and put out of the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator is useful when he contributes to the effect (economy, summary, general view). If the subject merely asks to be reflected or pictured, avoid an intervening narrator; an unneeded narrator may undercut immediacy. Example contrast: avoid unnecessary narrator in books like The Wings of the Dove where drama is enacted before the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic method: enact rather than recount
rubrics_metrics.description: An undramatic subject can be treated dramatically—make use of looks and gestures, express the story through them, leave them to enact it—and you have a story which in its manner is effectually drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the tale's progress lies in the consciousness of characters, present that inner life through visible/audible signs (gestures, looks, dialogue, staged scenes) instead of explicit interior narration. Examples: later Henry James novels, The Awkward Age when consistently dramatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial/omniscient method for panoramic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: A large, loose, manifold subject, extensive in time and space, is a pictorial subject and must be presented as a conspectus with the angle of vision assigned to the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broad chronicles (e.g., Thackeray, Balzac) the narrator must draw back for a general view from time to time; pure scenic presentation cannot cover vast time/space and multitudinous life. Use omniscience to summarize, provide continuity, and relate episodes across scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to the subject's scope and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject passes a certain point it exceeds the capacity of the straight and dramatic method; it is simply a question of amount, of quantity, of the reach of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide method by the scale and nature of the material: small, tightly-focused actions can be dramatized; vast, multi-period subjects need pictorial narration. Examples: Madame Bovary and The Ambassadors are pictured impressions where dramatization would not make the most of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency/homogeneity of method as a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel in which a single method is pursued throughout—denying the help of any other—achieves a consistency and homogeneity that is a real value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Awkward Age exemplifies the artistic advantage of strict adherence to one method (pure drama). Maintaining a consistent method gives the work a 'complete-ness and cleanness' and an unmistakable effect; but it is hard to achieve and may be a tour de force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express inner life through enacted behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the root of the matter is in behaviour, their behaviour will sufficiently express what is in their minds; motives are betrayed by visible and audible signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, show characters’ thoughts and sentiments through their actions and dialogue so that the story proceeds in the open and the reader infers inner states. Example: Nanda in The Awkward Age—her actions render her intelligence and manipulate the situation without interior exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of pure drama for background and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic scene is vivid and compact; but it is narrow, it can have no great depth, and the colour of the atmosphere can hardly tell within the space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the effect of the action depends upon its time and place, purely dramatic presentation risks failing to convey the outlying associations and background. In such cases supplement dramatic scenes with broader descriptive survey or narrator’s overview to establish context and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial preparation to propel and energize action
rubrics_metrics.description: A pictorial impression, wrought to the right pitch, will speed the work of drama—become an effective agent in the book, instead of remaining a mere decorative introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the scene and background (detailed setting, social environment) so that, when the drama begins, action carries the weight of its setting. Example: Balzac’s Maison Vauquer is elaborated until it supplies energy and meaning to the ensuing drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: narrator as a principle of economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Where other things are equal a direct view of the matter in hand is the best. But the narrator represents the great principle of economy, and is a value in himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narration when it economizes exposition—summarizing, connecting, or framing material more efficiently than scenic presentation would. But do not invoke narrator merely for convenience when it diminishes dramatic immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrator for authorial convenience or lazy omniscience
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an easy-going reliance on a narrator of some kind, a showman who is behind the scenes of the story and can tell us all about it. He seems to come forward in many a case without doing the story any particular service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let the narrator intrude simply because it is easier to 'say what you like' about characters. For subjects that would benefit from enacted scenes, forcing them into narration is an anti-pattern that may embarrass or weaken the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist's advantage: fix the manner as well as the words
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist, using scenic method, claims the advantage of ensuring the very best acting imaginable—the author creates the manner in which the words are spoken, as well as the words themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing scenes rather than a play, use stage-direction-like description and detailed presentation of manner to control tone, emphasis, and expression; this preserves your intended effect and avoids reliance on actors' interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict dramatic method is difficult—practical caution
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat a subject with the rigour of Henry James is extremely difficult... it must always be simpler for a story-teller to use his omniscience, to dive into the minds of his people for an explanation of their acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that purely dramatic novels are demanding; many writers default to mixed or narrative methods for pragmatic reasons. Attempt strict drama only when you can sustain its constraints and when the subject truly demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix methods pragmatically when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in dealing with a subject entirely dramatic, a novelist may well find reason to keep to his old familiar mixed method—circumspice: it would appear that he does so invariably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to combine scenic dramatization with pictorial/narrative passages when the background, history, or breadth of the subject requires it. Mixed method can supply context without sacrificing dramatic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overload foreground action with irrelevant background associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the characters in the remoter planes of the action... no more is expected than their value for the purpose of the action in the foreground. Whatever more they may bring will lie idle, will contribute nothing, and may even become an embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid importing irrelevant pasts or associations (e.g., recurring characters with extraneous histories) that distract from the focal story; background figures should only bring what is directly useful to the current action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose method according to whether story is action-based or psychological
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of the book being what it is, an action merely, and an action strictly limited in its scope, it requires no narrator. In contrast, a story concerned entirely with the impact of experience upon a mind may prefer pictorial or narrated methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the core is 'what they do' (favor drama/scenes) or 'what happens in minds over time' (favor narration, psychological presentation). Let the nature of the subject—action vs. inner development—dictate the dominant method.
